item.title: Buena Vista Social Club — Sun Sep 27, 1:00 PM — DPAC Presented by First Horizon
item.description:
A Remarkable Blend of Music, Dance and Heart It’s been years since legendary singer Omara Portuondo last entered a recording studio. Once known as the “Queen of Feeling,” her voice was celebrated throughout Cuba – until she vanished from the spotlight. But when an ambitious young record producer brings her a rare opportunity, the elusive diva must finally reckon with her past. Hailed as a “jaw-dropping, soul-stirring must see” (The Washington Post), the Tony® and GRAMMY® Award-winning BUENA VISTA SOCIAL CLUB™ is a journey through music and memory into the beating heart of Havana. A world-class company brings the story of the iconic album to thrilling life in this tale of big dreams, second chances, and music that needs no translation.

item.title: Healing Histories: A Trauma-Informed Approach to Confronting the Legacy of Racial Covenants — Tue Sep 29, 12:00 PM — Trent Drive Hall 040
item.description:
Throughout the 20th century, communities in many parts of the United States used racial covenants to codify neighborhood segregation, a structural legacy that continues to drive inequities in health and economic success today. In this Think Global panel, experts with backgrounds in history, education and social justice will explore how communities are confronting the ongoing impacts of this often-hidden history, a process that can be a powerful tool in building stronger communities that are better able to flourish and respond to adversity.
Panelists will describe the community engagement process of Mapping Prejudice, an internationally recognized research project that works with communities across the United States to mobilize volunteers to identify and map racial covenants. The discussion will explore how this process has created collective understanding and led to policy change in places such as Minneapolis, and how a trauma-informed approach is essential to empowering communities.

item.title: Learning in Networks Reading Group — Tue Sep 29, 12:00 PM — Gross Hall
item.description:
Learning in Networks Reading Group and Seminar Series: Tuesdays, 12pm in 330 Gross Hall; lunch included The institute focuses on fundamental questions in statistical inference, machine learning, causal inference, and optimization on networks, with particular emphasis on statistical-computational tradeoffs, message-passing algorithms, learning dynamics, and network-based market design. By fostering collaboration across disciplines, the institute aims to develop new mathematical and algorithmic foundations for understanding complex networked systems and their applications. The institute is led by collaborators Jiaming Xu, Alex Belloni, Fan Wei, Galen Reeves, and James Moody. Learn more: https://sites.duke.edu/learninginnetworks/
Source: Duke University

item.title: 🎤 Karaoke Night at The Tavern 🍻 — Sat Oct 3, 9:15 PM
item.description:
Discover Durham Together Looking for an actually fun night out in Durham? This is one of those spots where the whole place just clicks.
Huge bar. Pool tables. Darts. A full karaoke stage. And a crowd that’s there to have a good time — whether you’re singing, cheering people on, or just hanging with friends over drinks.
The karaoke here is genuinely awesome because people actually get into it. You’ll hear everything from pop punk and country to throwback rap, emo classics, rock anthems, and songs everyone ends up singing together by the end of the night.
No pressure to perform. No “serious singer” vibe. Just good energy, great people, and one of the most entertaining nights you can have in Durham.
Come solo, bring friends, grab a drink, play some pool, put your name on the list, or just enjoy the show. Either way, you’ll probably leave with a sore voice and a few new friends. 🎶

item.title: Climate Up Close — Sat Oct 10, 2:00 PM — Nature Research Center
item.description: Meet a panel of climate scientists and put your questions to them yourself. Join us for a presentation and Q&A with climate scientists from Climate Up Close in the SECU Daily Planet Theater. Climate Up Close works to inform and elevate the national conversation on climate change by explaining the scientific consensus clearly, without partisanship or policy prescriptions. They challenge both denialism and fatalism—the opposing extremes that too often distort climate discourse. Their team of working climate scientists travels to communities across the country so that people can see the evidence for themselves and put their questions directly to researchers. Each event features a 45-minute talk that maps the landscape of climate knowledge, sorting impacts like heat waves, sea level rise, and hurricanes along a spectrum from well understood to genuinely uncertain. item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Fri Dec 25 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Fri Dec 25, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Sat Dec 26 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description: The pace of production for new and existing synthetic chemicals is continually increasing, rapidly outpacing our capacity to assess risks of exposure to these substances. item.description:
Focusing on the role that deportation defense lawyers play in legitimizing the deportation regime, this talk addresses the responsibilities lawyers have when representing people within an unjust legal system. What does it mean for an immigration lawyer to genuinely earn the trust of undocumented communities and become an abogade de confianza? Borja explores how lawyers can work alongside families, community organizers, and participatory defense campaigns to challenge detention and deportation. So doing, they can help center the leadership of criminalized people by supporting mutual aid efforts, court watch projects, and freedom campaigns. Borja's public talk casts light on what effective immigration advocacy can look like and encourages us to rethink the conventional wisdom that good legal representation alone is enough to produce justice.

The small patient populations inherent to rare disease present unique challenges that increase the risk of obtaining inconclusive trial results. Addressing these challenges requires careful attention to statistical rigor while utilizing tailored approaches that are necessary to make medical product development feasible in this space. Reliable and timely evidence that relies on data from all available information is critically important to patients and families affected by rare diseases, making the optimization of clinical investigation design, conduct, and analysis a matter of both scientific and ethical urgency.
The workshop will focus on key statistical considerations for tailored approaches employed across the full arc of rare disease development programs

item.title: NHBA Bird Outing — Wed Oct 7, 7:30 AM
item.description:
For questions, contact Vern Bothwell at vernb2017@gmail.com. The location will be Flat River Waterfowl Impoundment, about 0.4 miles north of Jock Road. The coordinates are 36.127667, -78.832790.
This outing is sponsored by the New Hope Bird Alliance (formerly New Hope Audubon).
Outings usually last 2-3 hours. No reservations or sign-up needed. If there is a large turnout for any particular outing, we may split into two groups. We do recommend carpooling for families or friend pods; while we love pets, there is a ‘no-pet’ policy for bird outings. New birders and birders of all skill levels are welcome.
Please wear long pants, socks, and sturdy shoes (ticks and chiggers may be present). Sun and bug protection are also recommended. Bring snacks and water if you like. Heavy rain will result in cancellation.
Source: New Hope Bird Alliance

item.title: Incredible Science — Fri Oct 9, 1:30 PM — Downtown Raleigh
item.description:
Join us for an entertaining half hour of science experiments and demonstrations. Day-to-day topics vary but often include physics and chemistry demonstrations on inertia, buoyancy and electromagnetism. Enjoy natural science topics such as the incredible composition of beaver teeth or the amazing design and strength of birds’ eggs. This walk-up program is offered:
Wednesdays — 1:30pm Thursdays — 1:30pm Fridays — 1:30pm Saturdays — 12:30pm, 2pm
Location: Windows on the World on the 3rd floor of the Nature Exploration Center. Designed for ages 7 and up. No registration required.
Source: NC Museum of Natural Sciences
